concept.name: Order book
concept.definition: The collection of unexecuted buy and sell orders for a security maintained by a trading venue, organized by price level and priority. Its state evolves through order book events - limit-order submissions, market orders, and cancellations - which together drive short-horizon price changes (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 2014).
concept.intuition: It is the visible queue of supply and demand waiting to trade: who wants to buy, who wants to sell, at what prices, and how much.
concept.mechanics: Limit orders rest in the book until matched, cancelled, or expired; incoming marketable orders execute against the best opposing prices, removing liquidity. Data feeds disseminate the book as snapshots and event updates, from which quantities like imbalance and depth are derived.
concept.failure_modes: The displayed book understates true liquidity because of hidden, reserve, and off-exchange interest, and snapshot data miss intra-event dynamics. Book liquidity can also evaporate in stress as quotes are cancelled en masse.
concept.misconceptions: Size visible in the book is not committed liquidity; orders can be cancelled in milliseconds, so the book is an offer to trade, not a guarantee.
concept.example: A book shows five price levels per side; a 10,000-share market buy consumes the best offer and the two levels above it, moving the price up two ticks.

citations.source: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 'The Price Impact of Order Book Events', Journal of Financial Econometrics 12(1):47-88 (arXiv preprint)

citations.section: Price-time priority, tick size, and lot size
